lesson.title: Point-Slope Form: Writing a Line's Equation From Just a Point and a Direction
lesson.summary: Point-slope form builds a line's equation straight from one ordered pair and the slope, without ever needing to solve for the y-intercept first.
lesson.body:
Slope-intercept form is convenient once you know the y-intercept, but often a problem hands you a slope and some point on the line that is not the y-intercept, or it hands you two ordered pairs and expects you to find the equation between them. Point-slope form handles both situations directly. It is written as y minus y1 equals m times (x minus x1), where m is the slope and (x1, y1) is any known point on the line. Unlike slope-intercept form, it does not require knowing b at all.

The form comes straight from the slope formula. If (x1, y1) is a fixed known point and (x, y) represents any other point on the same line, the slope between them must equal m, so m equals (y minus y1) divided by (x minus x1). Multiplying both sides by (x minus x1) clears the fraction and gives y minus y1 equals m times (x minus x1), which is exactly point-slope form. It is really the slope formula rearranged so that a fixed point and the slope build the whole equation directly.

Try it with a line through the point (4, negative 2) that has slope one half. Substitute x1 = 4, y1 = negative 2, and m = 1/2 into the form: y minus (negative 2) equals 1/2 times (x minus 4), which simplifies to y plus 2 equals 1/2 times (x minus 4). To convert this into slope-intercept form, distribute the 1/2 across the parentheses: 1/2 times x is 1/2 x, and 1/2 times negative 4 is negative 2, giving y plus 2 equals 1/2 x minus 2. Subtract 2 from both sides: y equals 1/2 x minus 4. Check the original point by substituting x = 4: y equals 1/2 times 4 minus 4, which is 2 minus 4, equals negative 2, matching (4, negative 2) exactly.

Point-slope form is especially useful when you are given two ordered pairs instead of a slope directly. Take the points (1, 4) and (3, 10). First use the slope formula: m equals (10 minus 4) divided by (3 minus 1), which is 6 divided by 2, equals 3. Now pick either point, say (1, 4), and build the equation: y minus 4 equals 3 times (x minus 1). Distributing gives y minus 4 equals 3x minus 3, and adding 4 to both sides gives y equals 3x plus 1. Check it against the other point, (3, 10): y equals 3 times 3 plus 1, which is 9 plus 1, equals 10, confirming the equation is correct.

Because point-slope form only needs a slope and one ordered pair, it connects the slope formula, ordered pairs, and linear functions into a single, dependable procedure for writing any non-vertical line's equation.

One detail worth noticing is that either ordered pair from a pair of points will produce a correct, though differently arranged, equation before simplifying. Using the second point, (3, 10), instead of (1, 4) in the last example gives y minus 10 equals 3 times (x minus 3). Distributing, that is y minus 10 equals 3x minus 9, and adding 10 to both sides gives y equals 3x plus 1, the exact same simplified equation reached before. The unsimplified point-slope expression looks different depending on which point you pick, but once distributed and combined, it always settles into the same slope-intercept form, since both points describe the same line. This flexibility is part of why point-slope form is so often the first stop when a problem hands you raw ordered pairs rather than a ready-made y-intercept.
